item.title: COP17 faces test of turning biodiversity pledges into action
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
YEREVAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Four years after the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, its first global progress report has found uneven progress toward the 2030 targets, with the biggest gaps in efforts to address the drivers of biodiversity loss. The State of Biodiversity Action report, released by the United Nations on Thursday, will inform the first global review of collective progress under the framework at the upcoming 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) in the Armenian capital. With the conference opening on Oct. 19, the challenge is to turn the review's findings into concrete action. UNEVEN PROGRESS Countries have taken action across all 23 targets of the framework for 2030, but none presents an entirely positive picture, according to the report. Unless collective implementation accelerates, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved. The report identifies two gaps: national targets do not fully reflect the scope and ambition of global commitments, and implementation falls short even of those less ambitious targets. Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the CBD, said in August that fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties and aligned with the framework were on track. The largest gaps concerned resource mobilization, harmful subsidy reform, business impacts and the transition to sustainable consumption. Schomaker has noted promising conservation efforts, alongside slow progress on resource mobilization, harmful subsidy reform and inclusive governance. The framework calls for reducing incentives harmful to biodiversity, including subsidies, by at least 500 billion U.S. dollars annually by 2030. Yet an analysis by the Britain-based website Carbon Brief found that only about 5 percent of countries had set quantitative targets for subsidy reductions. Some countries reported that reform faced obstacles from vested interests and political resistance. ECONOMIC OBSTACLES A recent report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) points to tightening public finances and immediate pressures over food and energy security as reasons why some countries have shown insufficient political will for biodiversity protection. The problem becomes more acute when reforms affect powerful interest groups or impose immediate costs on certain sectors, while conservation benefits are shared across society and take longer to emerge. International financing presents another challenge. Under the framework, international biodiversity finance from developed countries and other contributors to developing countries was to reach at least 20 billion dollars annually by 2025, increasing to at least 30 billion dollars by 2030. However, the State of Biodiversity Action report shows that reported international public finance totaled only 17.7 billion dollars between 2020 and 2023, averaging about 4.4 billion dollars a year. An assessment by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services warns that delaying action could double the costs and increase the risk of irreversible losses, including species extinctions. Current economic models are also exacerbating biodiversity loss, climate change, water scarcity, food insecurity and health risks, with unaccounted-for costs estimated at 10 trillion to 25 trillion dollars annually. Within and between countries, the central tension is who should bear the immediate costs of protecting nature and when. The longer action is delayed, the greater the overall costs. TURNING REVIEW INTO ACTION The key test for COP17 is whether the review can provide clear guidance for further action, according to the Institute for Sustainable Development and International Relations, a French think tank. Under the convention's procedures, the global review materials will be submitted to COP17, where parties will examine implementation gaps and consider follow-up action. Observers say three questions will be central to the conference. First, what signals will its decisions send? Harmful subsidy reform and the integration of biodiversity into economic decision-making are among the areas lagging most. A general call to accelerate action would carry different weight from specific measures addressing these obstacles. Second, how will funding be secured and managed? Financing is a major weakness identified by the review and an important measure by which developing countries will judge the conference's outcome. The WWF has called on COP17 to deliver results rather than further promises, including a credible path toward mobilizing at least 30 billion dollars annually in international biodiversity finance by 2030. Third, how will supporting measures be implemented? At the Kunming Dialogue on the framework's implementation in September, participants broadly agreed that finance, capacity-building and technology were equally important. They also noted that support remained insufficient, while reliance on short-term funding hampered long-term planning and implementation. Despite the gaps exposed by the report, Schomaker has stressed that the 2030 targets remain achievable, provided major changes are made. COP17 will need to address who bears the costs of protecting nature and how to overcome resistance to reforms that bring short-term difficulties but long-term benefits. Its decisions will help determine whether the framework remains a set of commitments on paper or is translated into national budgets, subsidies and investment. ■

item.title: IMO chief urges ships to avoid Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
LONDON, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez has urged ships to avoid transiting the Strait of Hormuz and trading in the region as attacks on commercial vessels continue to escalate. He warned that safe shipping operations cannot resume until the underlying causes of the conflict are addressed. In an interview with Xinhua at the IMO headquarters in London on Friday, Dominguez said the organization's advice remained unchanged: ships should avoid transiting the Strait of Hormuz and trading in the region. "The situation continues to escalate," he said. He further said more than 110 vessels have been hit since the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran began in late February, while at least 24 seafarers have been confirmed dead. Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have intensified recently, with the security situation continuing to deteriorate, data published on the IMO website showed. A total of 12 attacks on vessels were reported in the strait and nearby waters between Oct. 5 and 11, the highest weekly figure since the conflict began. On Oct. 11 alone, six vessels came under attack. Dominguez cited two recent incidents to illustrate the increasingly serious consequences of the attacks. "Just in the last couple of days, we have two vessels that were hit, one a total loss, the other one still trying to reach a berth where it could be assisted," he said. Dominguez expressed concern that too many shipowners and operators continued to take risks despite the dangers. He warned that prolonged disruption to shipping could have wider consequences beyond the maritime sector. "It may have an even bigger impact when it comes to the global economy and supplies of energy sources as well as food security," he said. The IMO chief said the organization was continuing to support around 6,000 seafarers who had remained trapped in the region since the beginning of the conflict. However, Dominguez stressed that protecting seafarers must remain a priority, even if avoiding high-risk waters leads to higher costs. "Costs will increase globally; it's a reality, but we cannot put the lives of innocent seafarers at risk anymore," he said. Asked whether the IMO had been in contact with the parties involved in the conflict, Dominguez said the organization was maintaining communications with all its member states, particularly those directly involved, as well as countries beyond the region and other United Nations agencies. He acknowledged mediation efforts by several countries but said they had yet to produce the decisions needed to allow shipping operations to return to normal. "The root causes are not being addressed," Dominguez said. "So from our side, we can only work on the operational aspects of shipping, but it's been very clear that until the parties in the conflict sit down and find a solution to why this crisis started, we will not be able to resume operations safely around the region." On the protection of seafarers, Dominguez said the IMO was reviewing existing rules and guidance on risk assessments before vessels enter conflict zones or high-risk areas. The organization was also engaging with shipowners, operators and seafarers' representatives to explore ways to help seafarers obtain necessary supplies and uphold their rights under the Maritime Labour Convention. These include the right to refuse to transit dangerous areas without retaliation and the right to receive repatriation support. He said the IMO was also examining how existing regulations could be better enforced, including the detention of non-compliant vessels until they demonstrate compliance with international requirements. Dominguez noted that geopolitical conflicts were affecting shipping across several regions, including the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. Until these areas become more peaceful and shipping is no longer used as leverage in conflicts, vessels should avoid operating in such high-risk waters, he said. ■

item.title: Vocational education supplies nearly 10 mln skilled workers annually in China: white paper
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
The White Paper on Vocational Education in China is released during the closing ceremony of the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 17, 2026. The conference closed here on Saturday. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo) TIANJIN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- In recent years, China's vocational education system has provided an annual average of almost 10 million skilled personnel to various industries, according to a white paper released on Saturday. The white paper on China's vocational education was issued at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China, which ran from Thursday to Saturday this week. The white paper revealed that the average length of education among China's newly added skilled personnel had reached 14.35 years. In 2025, 5.82 million students graduated from higher vocational education institutions, while nearly 5.22 million graduated from secondary vocational schools, the white paper said. China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions. Higher vocational institutions account for more than half of the country's higher education institutions. In addition, 52 regular higher education institutions offer vocational undergraduate programs. As of the end of 2025, China's catalog of vocational education majors covered 19 major categories, 97 categories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories. At the Tianjin conference's closing ceremony, the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards, the development of which was led by China, was jointly released by 45 countries. The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing a lifelong education and training system for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams via school-enterprise partnerships, and using AI to drive reform in education and teaching. Four national standards for Luban Workshops, proposed by China's Ministry of Education, were also unveiled at the closing ceremony. They cover development requirements, teaching equipment requirements and operational quality assessment, among others. These standards will take effect on April 1, 2027. Luban Workshops are overseas vocational education projects jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, offering academic programs and skills training. China has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, which have provided academic education to more than 30,000 students and skills training to over 160,000 participants. ■ The closing ceremony of the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference is held in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 17, 2026. item.title: Chinese premier arrives in Uzbekistan for official visit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
TASHKENT, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived in Tashkent on Saturday for an official visit to Uzbekistan at the invitation of Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov. The traditional friendship between China and Uzbekistan has a long history, Li said, noting that the two countries are good friends, good partners and good brothers. Over the past 34 years since the establishment of diplomatic relations, China and Uzbekistan have always respected each other and treated each other as equals, regardless of changes in the international landscape, Li said. Bilateral relations and cooperation have continued to move forward, with new vitality and dynamism, he added. In recent years in particular, with the joint efforts of both sides, political mutual trust between China and Uzbekistan has become more solid, friendship has taken deep root in the hearts of the people, and practical cooperation has achieved fruitful results, delivering tangible benefits to the two peoples, said the premier. Li noted that Chinese President Xi Jinping and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev met in Bishkek not long ago and reached important consensus on further deepening bilateral relations. China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to translate the consensus reached by the two heads of state into more tangible outcomes, and deepen and strengthen the building of the China-Uzbekistan community with a shared future, Li added. On Li's arrival, the Uzbek prime minister and other senior government officials greeted him at the airport and held a welcome ceremony in his honor. ■

item.title: Xiplomacy: Xi's decades-long commitment to poverty reduction
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Poverty eradication is "a common ideal of humanity," Chinese President Xi Jinping has once said. Five years after China declared a complete victory in the fight against absolute poverty in 2021, its approach continues to inspire poverty reduction efforts worldwide. Xi's dedication to poverty alleviation spans decades, from his early work in poor rural communities to the nationwide campaign he led and his efforts to promote international cooperation -- a long-running endeavor that resonates as the world marks the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty on Saturday. A DECADES-LONG PURSUIT "A weak hatchling bird can be the first to fly, and the poorest can be the first to become rich," Xi wrote in a 1988 essay on the development of Ningde Prefecture in east China's Fujian Province. The following summer, Xi, then Ningde's Party secretary, traveled by car and on foot to reach Xiadang, a remote mountain township that had no road access. Xi returned to Xiadang twice, helping tackle problems with roads, electricity and water supplies. In 2019, residents wrote to tell him that their township had shaken off poverty, and he replied with congratulations. After becoming China's top leader, Xi continued his hands-on approach to poverty reduction. He conducted more than 50 inspections and research visits related to poverty alleviation, traveling to all 14 of the country's contiguous areas of extreme poverty. In February 2018, Xi visited impoverished Yi families in Zhaojue County, Sichuan Province, asking about their livelihoods and discussing ways to tackle poverty with villagers and local officials. "Not a single ethnic group or family should be left behind in building a moderately prosperous society in all respects," he said during the visit. On Feb. 25, 2021, Xi declared a "complete victory" in China's fight against absolute poverty. Over eight years, nearly 100 million rural residents had been lifted out of absolute poverty, enabling the country to meet the poverty reduction target of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development a decade ahead of schedule. In a congratulatory letter to Xi, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the achievement "a reason for hope and inspiration to the entire community of nations." LESSONS BEYOND BORDERS China's poverty reduction experience has attracted attention from leaders around the world, some of whom have sought inspiration from Xi's writings and visited places where his ideas were put into practice. Xi's early ideas on poverty reduction and economic development were collected in "Up and Out of Poverty," a collection of speeches, articles and interviews from 1988 to 1990 during his tenure in Ningde. Explaining the title, Xi wrote that its significance lay first and foremost in uprooting the "poverty mentality" and "poverty thinking." In a foreword to the book's Uzbek edition published in 2023, President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev said the work remained an important source of guidance for state and social governance more than three decades after its initial publication. During his visit to China this month, President of Botswana Duma Gideon Boko traveled to Fuzhou and Ningde in Fujian Province, where Xi once worked, and visited an exhibition on poverty reduction. During talks with Xi in Beijing, Boko depicted China's development as "an economic and political miracle never seen in history." In June 2018, Bounnhang Vorachith, then President of Laos, visited Shibadong Village in central China's Hunan Province to learn about China's approach to poverty reduction. In villager Shi Basan's home, he paused before a photograph showing Xi chatting with her beside a fire pit. During that November 2013 visit, Xi first proposed "targeted poverty alleviation" in a discussion with villagers, calling for measures tailored to local conditions and each household's needs. After retracing Xi's route and speaking with residents, Bounnhang voiced hope of bringing the village's experience back to Laos. In reply to a letter from the villagers the following year, he praised Shibadong's success as offering invaluable lessons for his country. In September 2026, Prime Minister of Madagascar Mamitiana Rajaonarison also visited Shibadong, where he witnessed first-hand residents' changing lives and watched demonstrations of traditional Miao ethnic embroidery. He said the visit shown him Xi's deep concern for the people and provided inspiration for Madagascar. TURNING EXPERIENCE INTO ACTION Xi's efforts to share China's poverty reduction experience abroad date back to his early tenure in Fujian Province. There, he promoted Juncao technology as part of Fujian's poverty reduction cooperation with northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. In 2000, he introduced the technology to a visiting governor from Papua New Guinea and later helped establish a China-aided Juncao demonstration base in the Pacific island country. Juncao technology uses grass to cultivate mushrooms and provide livestock feed. The technology has spread to more than 100 countries, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs. In Zimbabwe, farmer Mandiudza Masvongo has earned 330 U.S. dollars from selling mushrooms since taking up Juncao cultivation in June 2025. The proceeds have helped her start a small cleaning products business, which she said could mark a turning point in her life. Beyond agriculture, China's development assistance has also improved basic services and created opportunities for small businesses. In Cambodia's Tanorn village, a China-aided project brought better roads, clean water and solar power. Por Sokhim, once dependent on rice farming, now runs a grocery store, while her husband operates a motorcycle repair shop. In 2021, Xi proposed the Global Development Initiative, with poverty reduction and food security among its priorities. In the five years since its launch, cooperation projects under the initiative have taken root and delivered tangible results in more than 120 countries. At the 2024 G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro, Xi drew upon China's experience to express confidence in the prospects for poverty reduction across the developing world. "If China can make it, other developing countries can make it too. This is what China's battle against poverty says to the world," he told world leaders. ■

item.title: Xi stresses prioritizing ecological conservation, pursuing green development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, visits the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Oct. 16, 2026. Xi made an inspection trip on Friday to the city of Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yan Yan) ULANQAB, Inner Mongolia, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need to unswervingly follow the path of prioritizing ecological conservation and pursuing green development. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks during an inspection trip on Friday to the city of Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Huangqihai Lake in Ulanqab was once on the verge of drying up due to climate and other impacts. After years of comprehensive conservation, its water body has gradually been restored and expanded. During the inspection trip, Xi visited the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve, where he was briefed on Inner Mongolia's efforts to strengthen ecological conservation, and inspected the lake's shoreline and mudflats and observed birds inhabiting the area. He stressed the need to fully implement the country's wetland protection law, firmly uphold ecological red lines, and safeguard biodiversity. For degraded wetland ecosystems, he called for giving priority to natural restoration, supplemented by human intervention, and carrying out restoration in a scientific and sound manner. Xi visited Chahar High Tech Development Zone in Ulanqab, and learned about Inner Mongolia's progress in advancing the construction of a hub for the "East Data, West Computing" project and the development of the green computing power industry. Noting that implementing the "East Data, West Computing" project and building a national integrated computing power network is an important decision made by the CPC Central Committee, Xi stressed the need to ensure the efficient operation of completed projects and finish the construction of follow-up projects on schedule. He called on all parties to earnestly implement the requirements for efficient, green and safe development, actively promote the development of the green computing power industry, and make greater contributions to building Digital China and developing new quality productive forces. Xi also viewed displays of local agricultural and livestock specialties, encouraging local authorities to better align production with sales to help farmers and herders increase their incomes. ■ Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, talks with staff members while visiting Chahar High Tech Development Zone in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Oct. 16, 2026.
